papers.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
papers.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

papers.title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
papers.abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

papers.title: Towards end-to-end optimization in multimaterial 3D printing
papers.abstract: Multimaterial 3D printing enables the fabrication of functionally graded components, but optimizing their spatial material distribution alongside structural topology remains a formidable challenge due to high-dimensional design spaces and complex constitutive modeling. Using neural network constitutive laws in topology optimization requires their tangents and design sensitivities, which current approaches obtain by automatic differentiation through the network or derivation by hand. This paper combines sparsification, which reduces a trained physics-augmented neural network to a compact, interpretable closed-form law, with symbolic differentiation, enabling an end-to-end workflow from a new continuously varying multimaterial system to its mechanical simulation and design. By extracting closed-form, composition-aware hyperelastic constitutive laws from sparsified neural networks trained on experimental data, this approach facilitates exact symbolic differentiation of the terms required by the adjoint state method implemented with FEniCSx, circumventing the bottlenecks of applying neural network constitutive models in analysis and optimization. This pipeline is deployed on soft robotic gripper applications, demonstrating continuous composition optimization for highly anisotropic contact responses, and the concurrent optimization of macroscopic topology and material distribution under non-failure stretch constraints. This study is a step toward replacing conventional constitutive modeling and laborious empirical prototyping, establishing interpretable machine-learning models as practical, robust design primitives for advanced multimaterial additive manufacturing.

papers.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Sensitivity Analysis for Enhanced Structural Health Assessment: Test-Case for a Mixed Steel-Concrete Bridge
papers.abstract: Bridges are vital components of transportation systems, that serve as essential links ensuring the safe and efficient movement of people, goods, and emergency responders, especially during crises. With aging infrastructures, increasing traffic volumes and loads, and the intensifying impacts of extreme weather events due to climate change, the development of effective physics-informed structural health monitoring (SHM) frameworks has become critically important, more so when combined with sensitivity analysis (SA), which identifies the most influential structural parameters in the bridge's response. To support this, a high-fidelity, physics-based numerical model of a full-scale, two-span, mixed steel-concrete test bridge has been developed. This model serves as a virtual replica of a real structure located at the University of the Bundeswehr Munich. The numerical model is used as a complementary tool to improve prognostic capabilities and quantify uncertainty. A SA study is conducted to evaluate the structure's response under various mechanical conditions. Assessing these operational variations' effects on structural behavior forms part of an integrated, systematic evaluation framework aimed at combining SHM and SA.

papers.title: Model-Informed Joint Material-Structural Optimization of Hard-Magnetic Soft Materials
papers.abstract: This work develops a model-informed framework for predictive analysis and optimal design of hard-magnetic soft materials (hMSMs), which undergo contact-free, field-driven deformation. Accurate prediction requires effective structure-property relations, while optimal design requires coordinated control of structural density, magnetic particle distribution, and remanent magnetization direction. First, classical rigid-inclusion, Hill self-consistent, and constrained-kinematics models are placed in a unified effective shear-modulus framework for particle-filled elastomers. Six particle-fraction-dependent relations and one default control relation are combined with three strain-energy density functions to obtain 21 constitutive models. The results show that the strain-energy form has a relatively small effect for the actuation problems considered, whereas the effective shear-modulus relation can significantly affect deformation when magnetic material overlaps with substantially deforming regions. Experimental stress-strain data are used to select a representative shear-modulus relation, with the Mooney relation giving the lowest errors for the dataset and metrics considered. Second, the selected model is incorporated into a joint material-structural optimization formulation with separate fields for structural density, magnetic particle volume fraction, and remanent magnetization direction. The particle-fraction field affects both effective stiffness and magnetic loading, while the applied field is prescribed. Rotational, translational, restorative, and three-dimensional morphing examples demonstrate different active design fields, objectives, and single- or multi-load-case formulations, producing non-intuitive hMSM designs with prescribed deformation responses. The framework is implemented in the open-source CEADpx/MatTO repository.

papers.title: OpenTherm: A Unified and Progressive Benchmark for 2.5D/3D-IC Thermal Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient chip thermal prediction is essential for advanced packaging design. In recent years, deep learning-based thermal predictors have made significant progress, achieving high prediction accuracy while substantially reducing computational costs. However, differences in datasets, simulators, and evaluation protocols hinder direct comparison of existing methods and systematic assessment of their generalization across design variations and cross-package transfer scenarios. We introduce OpenTherm, an open benchmark combining 32,000 established 3D-IC samples with 50,000 new 2.5D chiplet samples generated with the open-source HotSpot simulator. It provides fixed data splits, a common input representation, and shared evaluation tools. Five deployment-aligned Generalization Scopes cover fixed-design workload prediction, within-family layout, material, and cooling exploration, and cross-package out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer with few-shot adaptation. Under a shared protocol, eight model configurations show gradual error growth within known package families. The best MAE increases by 13.7x from the broadest within-family scope to zero-shot cross-package transfer. Larger models do not consistently generalize better, and ten labeled fields per unseen package reduce MAE by 76-93%. Project site: https://github.com/Day333/OpenTherm.
